summary: Describes an architecture for secure firmware updates on resource-constrained Internet of Things devices. Updating is essential for fixing vulnerabilities, and also lets operators change configuration and add features.

plainLanguage.summary:
Small connected gadgets need a safe way to receive repairs. This RFC describes how that works: who makes the update, who stores it, who tells the device about it, and who checks it before it runs.

The check happens twice, once when the device downloads the update and again when the device restarts, so a tampered image is caught even if it got past the first check.

questions: how to securely update iot devices
what is iot firmware update architecture
how does a device verify a firmware update
what is an iot firmware update architecture
subtitle: An architecture for delivering and applying firmware updates to small, resource-constrained devices.

tldr.problem: Small devices need firmware updates to fix vulnerabilities, but they have little memory, no user to click a button and often no way to be reached. Updates also have to arrive safely, because a bad update is remote code execution by another name.
tldr.mechanism: A manifest describes the update and is signed by its author. A status tracker tells the device that an update exists, a firmware server hands over the manifest and the image, and a bootloader verifies the image again before running it.
tldr.outcome: The document is the architecture, not the format. The manifest format and the information model are specified separately in the IETF Software Updates for IoT working group, and this RFC points to them.

facts.label: Images held on a device
facts.value: At least three: bootloader, backup and new image

today: RFC 9019 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It is the architecture for the IETF Software Updates for Internet of Things working group. The manifest format itself is specified elsewhere, in the SUIT manifest and information model, and the RFC points readers to those for the details.

sections.title: Why Firmware Updates Need an Architecture
sections.content:
Firmware updates fix security vulnerabilities, so a secure update mechanism is a building block of a secure device. The Internet Architecture Board organised a workshop on Internet of Things software updates, RFC 8240, which surfaced a set of challenges and led to the creation of the IETF Software Updates for Internet of Things (SUIT) working group.

Building a secure small device is hard, and supporting updates takes skilled engineers. Once devices are deployed, updates matter for the whole life of the device, especially when it will live for years or sits somewhere that is expensive to reach. Updates for small devices are expected to happen automatically, without a user. Unlike a laptop, where a person is asked first, an unattended update is what makes it possible to fix vulnerabilities at scale.

Updates are not only for bugs. They also add features and reconfigure a device for a new environment. The manifest, the piece of metadata that describes an update, therefore has to allow for several things.

The firmware image must be authenticated and integrity protected, so that a modified image or one from an unknown source cannot be flashed. The examples use asymmetric cryptography because many deployments prefer it, but symmetric credentials are also supported, for very constrained devices.

The image may also be kept confidential, so that an adversary cannot easily recover the plain binary. Getting hold of the firmware is often the first step of an attack, because it reveals the libraries used, the configuration settings and the general functionality. Confidential protection is optional; authentication and integrity protection are not.

The RFC also lists the questions that fall outside standards work but matter to firmware authors and operators: installing updates so a failure does not brick the device, and offering recovery when an update goes wrong; getting updates out in time given the decision process, recertification and supply chain involved; keeping the update energy-efficient, since radio traffic and writing to flash are expensive on a battery; giving operators a reason to demand update support from vendors; and making sure critical fixes remain available after a product is discontinued or a vendor closes.
sections.plainLanguage:
Fixing a flaw in a small gadget is only useful if the fix can reach it. These devices are often unattended and far away, so the update has to arrive on its own.

Making that safe is the hard part, because installing an update is the same as letting someone run code on the device.

sections.title: The Roles in an Update
sections.content:
The RFC names five stakeholders. The author creates the firmware image, and there may be several authors behind the software on one device. The device operator runs a fleet of devices day to day and is the party users interact with, usually through a web page or a phone app. The network operator runs the network the devices connect to. The Trust Provisioning Authority (TPA) distributes trust anchors and authorisation policies to devices and to the other parties, and may delegate rights to them. It is usually the original equipment or design manufacturer, though a complicated supply chain may need a different arrangement, and a TPA may decide to keep the update process entirely under its own control. The user is the end user of a device.

Four functions carry the work.

The status tracker has a client and a server part and does three things: it tells devices that a new version is available, it passes information about the software and hardware characteristics of a device back to the server, and it can trigger an update remotely. The server part can sit in a cloud, on site, on an edge device, or even on one of the devices themselves, in which case the main microcontroller can act as the status tracker for the others. That is useful when updates have to be synchronised across several chips.

The firmware consumer receives the image and the manifest, parses and verifies the manifest, and stores the image. It plays the role of the update component on the device, usually inside the application firmware, and talks to the firmware server and to the local status tracker client.

The firmware server stores the images and manifests and distributes them. Some deployments need a store-and-forward arrangement, keeping the material on more than one entity on the way to the device. The firmware server and the status tracker usually interact, and are often on different machines for scale.

The bootloader is the piece of software that runs once a microcontroller has been reset and decides what code to execute.
sections.plainLanguage: Five organisations have a say, and four jobs get the work done: something that announces updates, something that stores them, something that downloads and checks them, and the bootloader that starts the new software.

sections.title: The Architecture and the Update Steps
sections.content:
More devices are connected than ever, so updates have to arrive over the Internet rather than through USB or a serial cable. That means the device fetches both the image and the manifest, and it needs certain components to do it: an Internet protocol stack for the download, with congestion control, flow control, fragmentation and reassembly, and a way to resume an interrupted or corrupted transfer; the ability to write the image to persistent storage, most likely flash; a manifest parser that can verify a digital signature or a message authentication code; the ability to unpack, decompress or decrypt the image; and a status tracker.

Most of that code lives in the application firmware rather than in the bootloader. Cryptographic algorithms, though, will usually run in a trusted execution environment on a separate chip, in a hardware security module or a secure element, rather than alongside the application.

In the architecture of Figure 1, the author creates an image and makes it available to a firmware server. For security, the author does not upload to the server or start an update directly; it makes the image available to the device operator instead. A longer supply chain may sit between the author and the party that finally authorises deployment.

First, the status tracker server tells the status tracker client that an update is available. That can happen by polling from the client, by a push from the server, or by a hybrid. Server-initiated updates matter because they react quickly, but they need the client to be reachable, which means keeping reachability information on the server side up to date and keeping the state at NATs and stateful packet filtering firewalls alive. The hybrid pushes the notification and then asks the firmware consumer to pull the manifest and the image from the firmware server.

The images and manifests may travel as a bundle or detached, and the manifest format must support both. A bundle, with the image inside the manifest, suits devices that are not on the Internet at all, or that are updated from a USB stick or a short-range radio. Detached delivery gives the consumer the manifest first and then lets the manifest say which images to fetch.

The remaining steps are: pre-authorisation, which checks whether the entity that signed the manifest is allowed to perform an update, and whether the consumer should fetch the image at all; dependency resolution, needed when more than one component can be updated or when a differential update is used, so that the dependencies are available before installation; the download, which may be client initiated, as with an HTTP/1.1 server, or server initiated, as when a manifest and image are pushed to the package resource of the LwM2M Firmware Update Object; the decision to install, which may wait for a trigger from the status tracker, happen automatically, or follow a more complex rule, and sometimes needs the user's confirmation; and installation, where the payload is processed into something the device recognises, after which the bootloader boots the new image.

Where no bootloader is involved, for instance when an application is updated in a full-featured operating system, the updater may halt and restart the application in isolation. Devices must not fail when a power cut or a network interruption happens during the update.
sections.plainLanguage:
The device learns that an update exists, fetches a manifest that describes it, checks the manifest, downloads the software, stores it and installs it.

The manifest can travel with the software or separately. Separately is more flexible, because the manifest then says where the software is.

sections.title: Starting the New Software and Recovering from Failure
sections.content:
Once the manifest and the image have been retrieved and processed, the new firmware has to be invoked. The usual pattern is to halt the running firmware, hand control to something with a higher privilege or trust level, the firmware verifier, which checks the new firmware's authenticity and integrity, and then start it. On a microcontroller that executes code in place, this means rebooting into the bootloader and running a secure boot process. In a rich operating system it may mean halting some processes and starting new applications, with the kernel checking the signatures on them.

This step is security sensitive, because an attacker will either try to pull a firmware image off the device to reverse engineer, or try to make the verifier run an image they have modified. The verifier's checks are in addition to the checks the firmware consumer made when it downloaded the material.

The two roles overlap in two ways. The verifier has to check the image it boots, which needs metadata stored alongside the image, and that metadata may be the same manifest that arrived with it. And a device needs a recovery strategy in case the update fails. That may mean keeping two or more application images on the device, or offering a recovery image that can fetch and install an update again over serial, USB or a short-range radio, in which case the firmware consumer functionality lives inside the recovery image, manifest parsing included.

On most devices the microcontroller has to restart to reach the bootloader. The bootloader then decides whether a newly available image should run. If it concludes the image is invalid, there are only two ways out: it must be able to select a different valid image, or it must be able to obtain new valid firmware. Both have architectural consequences. The first implies at least three images on the device: the bootloader itself, which is updatable and then treated like any other image; the image being replaced, kept as a backup in case the new one does not boot; and the newly downloaded image. The firmware consumer therefore has to know where to store the new firmware, sometimes implicitly, for instance by replacing the least recently used image, and sometimes explicitly. Because many low-end devices do not use position-independent code, the bootloader has to copy the new image into the old image's place and the old one back, or separate versions have to be prepared for each location. Generally the bootloader, or a minimal part of it, is not updated, since a failed bootloader update is a reliability risk.

For secure boot, the bootloader needs to fetch the manifest from non-volatile storage and parse it; to have hash functions, digital signature and message authentication code libraries available; to have a trust anchor store, or access to a key store for message authentication codes; to be able to expose boot-process data to the application firmware, so that the status tracker can report the current version and the state of the update; optionally to produce boot measurements for an attestation solution; and optionally to decrypt firmware images, which needs a key management solution.

The hardware varies, and the update has to cope. A single microcontroller with its own peripherals is the simplest and most common case, but its code is usually executed in place, so the image has to sit at a fixed place in flash and the old and new images have to be swapped. A single processor with a security partitioning scheme keeps two images, one for secure mode and one for normal mode, and must be able to update either on its own or both together atomically. A symmetric multiprocessor system, often running Linux with external storage, can usually keep several copies of the image and pick one to boot. Two processors sharing memory behave like the partitioned case. Two processors on separate buses each have to update their own firmware, usually with one acting as the master and directing the other, which makes an atomic update of both hard.
sections.plainLanguage:
The device restarts, and the bootloader checks the new software before running it. If the check fails, the device needs a way back: either an older good copy it can boot, or a recovery image that can fetch the update again.

The exact steps depend on the hardware. Some chips can only run code from one fixed place, so the old and new copies have to be swapped.

sections.title: What the Manifest Decides
sections.content:
To apply an update, the firmware consumer has to answer a list of questions, using the manifest and what it already knows about the device. The RFC sets out the questions and the information that answers them.

  • Should the device trust the author of the firmware? It looks at the trust anchors and the authorisation policies on the device.
  • Has the firmware been corrupted? It checks the digital signature or message authentication code covering the firmware image.
  • Does the update apply to this device? It checks the conditions carrying the Vendor ID, Class ID and Device ID.
  • Is the update older than the active firmware? It compares the sequence number in the manifest.
  • When should the device apply the update? It reads the wait directive.
  • How should the device apply the update? It reads the manifest commands.
  • What kind of binary is it? It reads the unpack algorithms.
  • Where should the update be obtained? It reads the dependencies on other manifests and the firmware image URI.
  • Where should the firmware be stored? It reads the storage location and the component identifier.

The sequence number carries a warning. A device that is handed an old but valid manifest and firmware must not be tricked into installing it, because a flaw in the old image may let an attacker take the device over.

Keeping the manifest parser small and simple matters for constrained devices, and since the same code may run in the bootloader, it can end up in the trusted computing base, the part of the system that everything else trusts.

A manifest can protect more than firmware. It can protect configuration data such as network credentials or the personalisation data that goes with particular firmware. Personalisation data shows why confidentiality matters between parties that both deliver to the same device. It is used with trusted execution environments, where trusted applications from different authors may need data such as payment information conveyed securely. The author of a trusted application does not want its code exposed to anyone else, and the user does not want their payment information exposed either.
sections.plainLanguage:
The manifest holds the answers a device needs: who signed the update, whether it applies to that device, whether it is newer than what is installed, when to install it and where to put it.

The same list can protect configuration data and personal details, not just the firmware itself.

sections.title: Securing the Update Itself
sections.content:
Securing the update mechanism matters as much as the updates themselves, because a problem in the update process makes things worse, not better. An update is authorised remote code execution, so any weakness in the process exposes that remote code execution system, and failing to secure the process helps attackers take over devices.

End-to-end protection of the image and the manifest rests on three things. Authentication lets the device identify cryptographically the authors of images and manifests. Not every party that signs has the same permissions, so the device has to work out whether the requested action is covered by the permission of the party that signed. Telling the device about those permissions happens out of band, and is the duty of the Trust Provisioning Authority. Integrity protection stops anyone else modifying the manifest or the image. To accept an update, a device verifies the signature covering the manifest. There may be one manifest or several, potentially signed by different parties, so the device needs the trust anchors to check those signatures, and they are installed out of band before the update process begins. Confidentiality protection of the image must mean that nobody except the intended consumer and other authorised parties can decrypt it, and the per-device encryption must still work with content delivery networks, bulk storage and broadcast. The author needs the certificate, public key or pre-shared key of the device. Confidential protection of firmware images is optional.

The manifest specification has to support different cryptographic algorithms and be extensible. Because signature schemes based on RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography may become vulnerable to quantum-accelerated key extraction, bootloader code that cannot be changed, because it is in read-only memory, is advised to use post-quantum secure signature schemes such as hash-based signatures. The RFC puts the worst-case estimate for the time horizon to key extraction with quantum acceleration at approximately 2030, based on current research.

Where a device gets a single monolithic image from a single author with no extra approval, the authorisation flow is simple. Other cases need more policy. The architecture separates the authorisation policy from the communication architecture by separating entities from their permissions. An author may have no authority to install an image on a device in critical infrastructure without the device operator's authorisation, in which case the device can be programmed to reject updates unless they are signed by both. Alternatively, a device may trust one entity that does all the permission management, which lets it hand the complex calculations to somebody else.
sections.plainLanguage:
An update is a way to run new code on a device, so the update channel itself has to be locked down. The device checks who signed the update, checks that nothing changed on the way, and checks that the signer was allowed to do this.

Keepers of devices that live for years are advised to use signature schemes that will not be broken by quantum computers.

items.title: Author
items.text: Creates the firmware image and signs the manifest.

items.title: Firmware server
items.text: Stores the images and manifests and distributes them.

items.title: Status tracker
items.text: Announces that a new version exists and can trigger the update.

items.title: Firmware consumer
items.text: Parses and verifies the manifest and stores the image on the device.

items.title: Bootloader
items.text: Runs after a reset, checks the image and decides what code to execute.
